title: A card game that counts rising runs
hook: Deal eight cards into piles. The number of piles answers a question you never asked.

doesNotKnow: that a card game finds the longest rising run with skips

misconception: The longest rising sequence starts at the smallest number.
objective: The learner can explain that dealing 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 onto the leftmost pile whose top is not smaller makes 4 piles, that a rising run uses at most one card per pile, and that back-pointers give a run as long as the number of piles, so the longest rising run has 4 cards (e.g. 3 4 5 9 or 1 4 5 6).

claims.text: Dealing 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 onto the leftmost pile whose top is not smaller makes 4 piles.
claims.source: Builder's node script (scratchpad checks/all.mjs): piles [3,1,1] [4,2] [5] [9,6]. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Own node deal: [3,1,1] [4,2] [5] [9,6].

claims.text: The longest rising run (each card bigger than the last, skipping allowed) in 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 has 4 cards, for example 1 4 5 6 or 3 4 5 9.
claims.source: Builder's node dynamic programming over the 8 cards: longest strictly increasing subsequence length 4. Both examples checked by hand against the order of the cards. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Own O(n^2) DP: LIS = 4; 1 4 5 6 and 3 4 5 9 are both increasing subsequences in order (node).

claims.text: A longest rising run need not start at the smallest card.
claims.source: 3 4 5 9 has length 4, the maximum (c2), and starts with 3 while the smallest card is 1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Follows from c2: 3 4 5 9 is maximal and starts at 3, not the minimum 1.

claims.text: A rising run can use at most one card from each pile, since each pile goes downward.
claims.source: Cards on a pile are placed on tops not smaller than themselves, so each pile is non-increasing from bottom to top in deal order; two cards of a strictly rising run cannot both lie on one pile. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Piles are non-increasing; a strictly increasing run cannot take two cards from one pile (equal 1s included).

claims.text: Every card on pile k has an arrow back to a smaller, earlier card on pile k − 1, as your trace drew, so a run as long as the number of piles always exists.
claims.source: When a card lands on pile k, the top of pile k - 1 is smaller (else the card would have gone there) and was dealt earlier. Aldous and Diaconis, 'Longest increasing subsequences: from patience sorting to the Baik-Deift-Johansson theorem', Bull. AMS 36 (1999). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Back-pointer argument re-derived; own node check: piles = LIS length on 20,000 random sequences with repeats. Aldous and Diaconis, Bull. AMS 36(4) (1999). Stage trace from pile 4 gives 1 4 5 6. | REVISED v3 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): Reveal now points at the back-link arrows the trace draws between piles (r5: nothing on stage drew a pointer, and the old top-card '←' collided with 'points back'). Top cards are now marked by a heavy outline and 'pile k · top' header instead of '←'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Pass 22 re-check of v3: own deal: piles [3,1,1] [4,2] [5] [9,6]; every card's back-link (top of pile k-1 when it landed) is smaller and earlier (asserted in node). Reveal wording matches stage: arrows drawn only along the traced run. Aldous & Diaconis 1999 not re-opened (carried from pass 10).

claims.text: Deal captions, one per card: '<card> → pile k: top t is not smaller; u on pile k − 1 was', '<card> → pile 1: top t is not smaller', or '<card> → a new pile: every top is smaller'. For 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 these give 3 new, 1 on 3, 4 new, 1 on 1, 5 new, 9 new, 2 on 4 (1 on pile 1 was smaller), 6 on 9 (5 on pile 3 was smaller).
claims.source: why() in Demo.tsx, computed from the same place()/target() that build the piles. 'Deal the rest' now plays the remaining cards one per 0.9 s with these captions (r5 top finding: 7 of 8 rule applications were hidden). | REVISED v3 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): new sentence. New stage text. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Pass 22: own deal captions: 3 new (no piles yet), 1 on 3, 4 new, 1 on 1, 5 new, 9 new, 2 on 4 (1 on pile 1 was smaller), 6 on 9 (5 on pile 3 was smaller). Matches why() in Demo.tsx. Note: the first card uses a fourth template, "3 → a new pile (no piles yet).", which the claim does not list; it is true.

claims.text: Trace caption: 'Pile 4 back: 6 → 5 → 4 → 1. Each arrow: the smaller top on the pile to the left when that card landed.' Pile 1 has no pile to its left.
claims.source: place() in Demo.tsx stores prev = the top of pile k − 1 at the moment a card lands on pile k; since pile k is the leftmost whose top is not smaller, that top is smaller and earlier. Trace from pile 4 follows 6 → 5 → 4 → 1 (builder hand-check of the deal). | REVISED v3 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): new sentence. New stage text. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Pass 22: own back-links: pile 4 traces 6 -> 5 -> 4 -> 1 (the first 1, card 2), pile 3 5 -> 4 -> 1, pile 2 2 -> 1, pile 1 just its top. Caption strings match traceFrom() in Demo.tsx.

recall.question: You deal a row of cards into piles, each card on the leftmost pile whose top is not smaller, and end with 6 piles. What does that tell you?
options: The longest rising run (with skips) has 6 cards
There are 6 cards smaller than the first
recall.why: A rising run takes at most one card from each pile, and the back-pointers always build a run with one card per pile, so the pile count is the longest run's length.
